nameStory: This millipede earned its "traveling" name from its remarkable habit of forming massive groups that move together across the landscape like a slow-motion parade. The "cherry" part comes from its membership in the cherry millipede family, named for their often reddish coloration that resembles cherry wood. Imagine stumbling upon thousands of these little arthropods all marching in the same direction - it's like witnessing nature's own migration!
description: The traveling cherry millipede is a flat-backed, worm-like creature with many pairs of legs that moves in a slow, wave-like motion. Like all millipedes, it's a decomposer that helps break down dead plant material in the forest. These millipedes are highly variable in color, ranging from pale yellow to deep reddish-brown or even dark purple. They're typically about 1-2 inches long when fully grown and have a flattened body that's wider than it is tall.

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Flattened, ribbon-like body that's distinctly wider than it is tall, feeling firm but flexible when gently handled

idTips.label: Color variation
idTips.description: Extremely variable coloration from pale yellow to cherry red to deep purple-brown, often with lighter leg segments

idTips.label: Movement pattern
idTips.description: Slow, undulating motion with legs moving in coordinated waves, often curling into a tight spiral when disturbed

idTips.label: Group behavior
idTips.description: Occasionally found in large aggregations moving together in the same direction across trails or open areas

idTips.label: Size and segments
idTips.description: Adult length of 1-2 inches with approximately 20 body segments, each bearing two pairs of short legs

idTips.label: Defensive response
idTips.description: When threatened, releases a mild almond-like chemical smell and curls into a tight coil with head protected in the center

habitat: Look for these millipedes in deciduous and mixed forests with rich, moist soil full of decomposing leaves and organic matter. They prefer areas under logs, rocks, and leaf litter where humidity stays high, particularly in oak-hickory and maple forests. While rare in New England, they'd most likely be found in southern Connecticut's warmer, well-drained woodlands.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and soil moisture increases from snowmelt. Look under logs and in deep leaf litter where they're feeding on decomposing organic matter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they may be found wandering more openly, especially after rain. This is when the famous mass migrations are most likely to occur.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek deeper shelter. Good time to find them under thick leaf litter as they prepare for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, burrowed deep in soil or under logs and rocks where they remain dormant until spring temperatures return.

funFact: In 1950, researchers discovered about 6,000 traveling cherry millipedes all moving together across a single bridge in Indiana - imagine that slow-motion stampede of tiny legs all heading in the same mysterious direction!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other cherry millipedes in the Apheloria and Brachoria genera due to mimicry, but the traveling cherry millipede's highly variable coloration and occasional mass movement behavior help distinguish it. Remember: if you see a group of flat millipedes all traveling together like they're following a leader, you've likely found the traveling species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "cherry" millipedes, the family name refers to their coloration rather than any association with cherry trees. The extreme color variation in this species is thought to be a form of Müllerian mimicry, where multiple species share similar warning colors to reinforce the message to predators that they taste bad.
compareHints: This is the only Pleuroloma species recorded in New England, making it unique in the region. Compared to other cherry millipedes like Apheloria species, the traveling cherry millipede shows much more dramatic color variation within the same population and has the distinctive mass movement behavior. It's also the most widely distributed cherry millipede in North America, giving it the broadest range of any species in its family.
